course.title: Khaemenes Academy Kindergarten — 36 Unit A+ Curriculum
course.subtitle: Universal Kindergarten Readiness · In-House Curriculum · Play-Based Honors Foundation
course.dependencyPolicy: No outside fonts, scripts, images, libraries, or curriculum calls. All pages use local files only.
course.localReviewNote: Designed to surpass any single-state checklist by covering broad early-learning domains. Families, schools, or evaluators should still review local compliance requirements.

standardsFamilies.label: Developmentally Appropriate Practice
standardsFamilies.description: Play-based, strengths-based, joyful, engaged learning across whole-child domains.

standardsFamilies.label: Whole-Child Early Learning Domains
standardsFamilies.description: Approaches to learning, social-emotional development, language/literacy, cognition, motor and physical development.

standardsFamilies.label: Kindergarten Literacy
standardsFamilies.description: Oral language, print concepts, phonological awareness, alphabet knowledge, shared reading, drawing/writing, speaking/listening.

standardsFamilies.label: Kindergarten Mathematics
standardsFamilies.description: Counting/cardinality, comparing, sorting, composing/decomposing, measurement, data, geometry, patterning, problem solving.

standardsFamilies.label: Kindergarten Science and Engineering
standardsFamilies.description: Observation, weather/sunlight, living things, water/earth, motion, tools, safe inquiry, design, and evidence.

standardsFamilies.label: Early Social Studies and Civic Belonging
standardsFamilies.description: Family, community, maps, places, helpers, traditions, symbols, citizenship, needs/wants, and shared responsibility.

standardsFamilies.label: Social-Emotional Learning
standardsFamilies.description: Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, responsible decisions, kindness, and repair.

standardsFamilies.label: Arts, Music, Drama, and Creative Process
standardsFamilies.description: Creating, presenting, responding, connecting, rhythm, movement, visual design, storytelling, and reflection.

standardsFamilies.label: Health, Movement, and Safety
standardsFamilies.description: Gross/fine motor, body care, rest, nutrition, hygiene, movement, safe routines, and confidence.

standardsFamilies.label: Tools, Technology, and Unplugged Thinking
standardsFamilies.description: Sequencing, patterns, safe tool use, unplugged coding, digital citizenship, design, and creation.

lessons.title: Wonder Launch
lessons.duration: 45–75 minute flexible learning block plus centers
lessons.objective: Recognize your name, identify a feeling, and count a small group of classroom objects.
teacherScript: Invite learners to share, point to, draw, sign, or select what they already notice about welcome to the learning garden.
Introduce the unit question: “Who am I in this learning community?” and model one answer using concrete materials or pictures.
Model the literacy focus: Names, print awareness, listening routines. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly.
Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Count, match, and sort classroom objects. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC.
Close by asking each learner to communicate one observation, question, or idea; note what needs modeling tomorrow.

lessons.workshop: Introduce the unit question, vocabulary, read-aloud, song/movement routine, and shared anchor chart.

Shows the target skill on a concrete or pictured example using an accessible response mode.

instructionalQuality.prerequisiteCheck: Entry baseline: do not assume formal preschool skills. Invite an informal observation of communication, name recognition, object matching, and participation preferences.
instructionalQuality.explicitModel: Think aloud while solving one worked example. Name the clue, model each step, and connect the result to the learning target.
instructionalQuality.guidedPractice: Model the literacy focus: Names, print awareness, listening routines. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly. Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Count, match, and sort classroom objects. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC. Use gradual release: teacher demonstrates, solve together, learner attempts a parallel item with prompts, then fade prompts as ready.
instructionalQuality.misconceptionCorrection: Names and pictures communicate different information; model how each functions.
instructionalQuality.transferTask: Use a new object, picture, word, or scenario to check the prerequisite skill before the main teaching example. Tie the check to "Learning identity and help-seeking" and "Name and belonging"; use different surface details from the modeled example while preserving the core concept.
instructionalQuality.assessmentEvidence: Collect an observable sample for "Learning identity and help-seeking" and a reasoning sample for "Name and belonging". Record the child's response mode, prompts, and supports; participation alone does not prove mastery.
instructionalQuality.reteachIfNeeded: If the learner is not yet successful, model one step, reduce the choice set, use concrete objects and visual schedules, and record which supports helped; do not require public disclosure. Then model a smaller step, correct the misconception above, and try a new parallel item. Record which support helped; do not restart the whole lesson automatically.
instructionalQuality.target: Recognize your name, identify a feeling, and count a small group of classroom objects.

lessons.title: Guided Skill Lab
lessons.duration: 45–75 minute flexible learning block plus centers
lessons.objective: Sort classroom materials by what they are used for and explain where they belong.
teacherScript: Quickly revisit Monday’s vocabulary and show one worked example connected to welcome to the learning garden.
Model the steps for names, print awareness, listening routines; say or show what to notice before asking learners to try.
Guide learners through count, match, and sort classroom objects using manipulatives, pictures, movement, or other accessible tools.
Give each learner a new example and gradually reduce prompts; ask “What helped you decide?”
Record one successful strategy and one misconception to revisit during Wednesday’s investigation.

lessons.title: Create & Communicate
lessons.duration: 45–75 minute flexible learning block plus centers
lessons.objective: Use simple symbols to represent classroom spaces and choose one helpful responsibility.
teacherScript: Review the essential question and select one idea from the literacy, mathematics, or inquiry work to apply.

units.title: Names, Letters, and Stories
units.theme: Alphabet awareness, print concepts, oral storytelling, and counting collections
units.essentialQuestion: How do letters and stories help us share who we are?
units.literacyFocus: Name letters, environmental print, story parts
units.inquiryFocus: Books, authors, illustrators, characters, and settings

lessons.title: Wonder Launch
lessons.duration: 45–75 minute flexible learning block plus centers
lessons.objective: Identify or match familiar letters in the learner's name and explain or show that a familiar label or sign carries meaning.
teacherScript: Invite learners to share, point to, draw, sign, or select what they already notice about names, letters, and stories.
Introduce the unit question: “How do letters and stories help us share who we are?” and model one answer using concrete materials or pictures.
Model the literacy focus: Name letters, environmental print, story parts. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly.
Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Count to 10 with one-to-one correspondence. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC.
Close by asking each learner to communicate one observation, question, or idea; note what needs modeling tomorrow.

instructionalQuality.prerequisiteCheck: Builds on Week 1 name/label noticing, listening routines, object matching, and one-to-one counting; establish these with a quick baseline if not yet secure.
instructionalQuality.explicitModel: Think aloud while solving one worked example. Name the clue, model each step, and connect the result to the learning target.
instructionalQuality.guidedPractice: Model the literacy focus: Name letters, environmental print, story parts. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly. Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Count to 10 with one-to-one correspondence. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC. Use gradual release: teacher demonstrates, solve together, learner attempts a parallel item with prompts, then fade prompts as ready.
instructionalQuality.misconceptionCorrection: A name, a letter, a word, and a picture are related but different.
instructionalQuality.transferTask: Use a new object, picture, word, or scenario to check the prerequisite skill before the main teaching example. Tie the check to "Name-letter recognition" and "Letter and sound relationship"; use different surface details from the modeled example while preserving the core concept.
instructionalQuality.assessmentEvidence: Collect an observable sample for "Name-letter recognition" and a reasoning sample for "Letter and sound relationship". Record the child's response mode, prompts, and supports; participation alone does not prove mastery.
instructionalQuality.reteachIfNeeded: If the learner is not yet successful, start with the learner's own name or a highly familiar label; avoid guessing at untaught letter-sound correspondences and accept pointing, matching, dictation, or AAC. Then model a smaller step, correct the misconception above, and try a new parallel item. Record which support helped; do not restart the whole lesson automatically.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 10 · Maps, Places, and Community Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Explains that a map is a selective representation of a place and identifies something it leaves out.
Creates or decodes consistent symbols using a legend or key that does not rely only on color.
Uses positional or directional language accurately from a stated start or orientation and sequences a usable route.
Measures or compares route distance using one consistent model unit rather than body-dependent stride length.
Compares two routes using the same unit and explains a meaningful difference.
Knows that home address, live location, school route, bus stop, exact neighborhood, or identifying landmark is never required.
Designs or interprets a fictional community map and explains a safety or accessibility choice.
Explains that maps are made for purposes and can represent the same place differently.
Tests a map or route, identifies ambiguity or exclusion, and revises or explains a correction.
Uses a map, key, route, and privacy or access principle together.

verticalAlignment.next: Prepares for Week 11's model-and-measure approach to plant growth and later route/system reasoning.
verticalAlignment.support: Use fictional places and avoid personal home-location details; provide tactile, high-contrast, or verbal route alternatives.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 11 · Plants and Gardens Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Identifies common plant structures such as roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, or seeds and gives an age-appropriate function for at least two, without requiring every plant to have every part visible.
Explains that plants need suitable access to water, light, air, space, and appropriate growing conditions; avoids the misconception that soil itself is plant food.
Orders an age-appropriate seed/germination/growth sequence while recognizing that different plants grow at different rates and not every seed germinates.
Measures or compares plant/model growth from a consistent baseline using the same nonstandard unit or another accessible repeated measure.
Records at least two dated or ordered observations using drawing, marks, labels, dictation, photos of the plant only when appropriate, or another accessible evidence form.
Distinguishes what was observed from what is predicted and revises a prediction when evidence changes.
Identifies that changing one condition at a time makes a comparison more informative, using a safe model, teacher demonstration, or hypothetical example.
Uses adult guidance for unknown plants/seeds, avoids tasting classroom specimens, washes hands as appropriate, and uses choking/allergy-safe alternatives.
Demonstrates developmentally appropriate care for a living plant or uses a nonliving model when live-plant care is unavailable.
Explains one observation, measurement, or revised idea about how plants grow.

verticalAlignment.before: Builds on Weeks 4–6 observation, description, and data recording.
verticalAlignment.deepen: Move from naming plant parts/needs to recording change from a consistent baseline and distinguishing observation from prediction in a fair comparison.
verticalAlignment.transfer: Interpret two dated plant drawings or measurements and explain one supported change and one unanswered question.
verticalAlignment.next: Prepares for Week 12's animal structure/function and habitat-resource explanations.
verticalAlignment.support: Use supplied growth records if a plant has not grown; avoid implying that one short observation proves a general causal rule.

items.prompt: Gives an evidence-based observation about an animal structure or behavior and distinguishes it from a guess, personality label, or human-like story.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 17 · Winter, Light, and Shadows Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Identifies a light source, blocking object, and receiving surface/screen and explains that an opaque object can block light to produce a darker shadow region.
Changes one light/object/screen condition at a time, observes the resulting shadow change, and uses evidence to confirm or revise a prediction.
Explains that shadow size, position, or outline can change with source/object/screen geometry without claiming that the object itself grew or shrank.
Measures and compares modeled shadow lengths from a common baseline using equal repeated units and communicates number plus unit.
Identifies an unfair shadow measurement or model limitation such as shifted starts, mixed units, gaps/overlaps, or overgeneralizing one classroom setup.
Uses a globe/ball and fixed-light model to explain that Earth’s rotation produces the repeating day/night pattern, rather than teaching that the Sun travels around Earth each day.
Compares seasonal or daylight information with location-aware language and rejects the claim that winter universally means snow, freezing weather, or identical daylight patterns.

Knows never to look directly at the Sun and never requires lasers, flames/candles, high-heat lamps, electrical disassembly, lights aimed at eyes, unsafe darkness, or unsupervised night/outdoor observation.

Uses safe visual, tactile, modeled, signed, AAC, audio-described, partner-supported, or adult-scribed pathways without making standing, visual acuity, flashlight handling, or fine-motor tracing prerequisites.
Integrates shadow formation, one controlled change, fair measurement, Earth-rotation reasoning, and one corrected misconception or model limitation in an accessible explanation.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 20 · Stories Around the World Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Distinguishes story content from source/version information and recognizes that a teller, author, translator, adapter, reteller, or uncertain oral history may stand behind a particular version.
Uses careful one-version/uncertain-origin language and rejects the claim that one story represents every member of a culture, country, language, religion, or people.
Identifies character, setting, and beginning/middle/end or first/next/last using evidence from a provided story without treating fictional setting as a description of all real people.
Compares two stories or versions with at least one supported similarity and difference and names a conclusion the comparison does not justify about real people or places.

Counts a stated feature in a small provided story set with one-to-one correspondence and interprets or builds a simple comparison/graph without generalizing the sample to cultural worth or creativity.

Uses a map/key or positional language for documented or fictional story context and explains at least one limitation, including that borders do not define one culture, language, ancestry, religion, or way of life.
Recognizes translation/retelling as legitimate versions and does not rank oral, written, signed, illustrated, sung, digital, AAC, or performed storytelling as more or less civilized.

Identifies a motif or version change, avoids treating a shared motif as proof of common origin, and creates or explains an original variation using clearly appropriate classroom material rather than identity imitation.

Knows not to copy, reenact, remix, costume, or craft sacred/restricted Indigenous, religious, ceremonial, funerary, initiation, or community-protected material and knows no learner must disclose heritage or speak for a group.
Integrates source/version reasoning, story evidence, fair sample mathematics, map/place limits, uncertainty, and a cultural-respect boundary in an accessible explanation or model.

items.prompt: Uses more than one relevant evidence clue to reason about whether an example is a living organism and explicitly rejects movement, growth, energy use, or appearance alone as proof of life.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 22 · Water, Ice, and Weather Changes Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Identifies ice as solid water, liquid water as liquid H₂O, and water vapor as gaseous water while explaining that a state change does not make water a different substance.

Explains that water vapor is ordinarily invisible and that visible mist, fog, clouds, or the white plume near hot water consists mainly of tiny liquid droplets and/or ice crystals rather than visible gaseous water itself.
Sequences melting from solid to liquid and freezing from liquid to solid and rejects the idea that cold enters water as a material substance.
Identifies or uses a fair melting/freezing comparison with a stated variable and reasonably controlled starting amount/size, container, observation interval, or measurement method.
Explains that liquid water can evaporate into invisible water vapor below the boiling point and that drying does not mean the water simply ceased to exist.
Explains that water vapor can change to liquid droplets under suitable cooling conditions and correctly interprets a cold-surface condensation example without assuming leakage.
Explains that clouds contain tiny liquid droplets and/or ice crystals and that cloudiness does not guarantee precipitation; recognizes that precipitation form depends on conditions.
Reads or builds a small weather-water data display, makes an evidence-supported comparison, and names a sample/forecast/location or classroom water-cycle-model limitation.

Knows that mastery does not require boiling water, flame, hot plates, dry ice, liquid nitrogen, salt/ice skin experiments, tasting, walking on ice, home freezers, snow, or unsafe cold exposure; accessible models/data are valid evidence.

Integrates water-state identity, melting/freezing, evaporation/condensation, cloud/weather evidence, a fair-comparison idea, one misconception correction, a model/data limitation, and a safety boundary.

weeklyAssessment.title: Week 23 · Earth Care and Stewardship Mastery Evidence

items.prompt: Uses provided material, item-condition, contamination/special-handling, and local-rule evidence to choose an appropriate pathway such as use longer, reuse/repair, accepted recycling, managed composting, special handling, disposal, or check-the-rule.
Explains that a recycling symbol or recyclable material does not guarantee local program acceptance and uses the stated local/classroom guide rather than appearance or wishful guessing.

States the provided sorting rule before classification, applies it consistently, and uses check-the-local-rule/adult-special-handling when material, condition, contamination, or acceptance is uncertain.
Tallies a clean provided sample once per item, builds or interprets an accessible graph, verifies category totals against sample size, compares categories, and limits claims to that sample.

Compares at least two material strategies under a stated constraint, recognizes that reduce/reuse/repair are not universally best or safe, and revises the choice when a safety, access, hygiene, condition, or local-system fact changes.

Knows that stewardship mastery never requires handling real trash, sharps, glass, batteries, e-waste, chemicals, medicine/medical waste, moldy food, animal waste, unknown containers, or denying needed health/disability/sanitation/safety supplies.

Explains that material and environmental outcomes involve design, production, infrastructure, public agencies, facilities, workers, schools, households, and community rules and are not a moral burden placed on children or one family alone.
Uses documented fictional place evidence to identify a problem/need, separates observation from assumptions about who caused it, and rejects blaming a person/community without evidence.

Chooses stewardship actions that avoid feeding/chasing/moving wildlife and avoid independent hazardous litter collection, using adult reporting, protected space, design, or properly organized cleanup instead.
Integrates local-rule classification, checked data, material-strategy tradeoffs, dignity, system responsibility, shared-place evidence, a safe action, and a way to evaluate improvement.

items.prompt: Identifies a push or pull as an interaction and connects it to an observed change in motion such as starting, stopping, speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction without treating force as a substance stored in an object.
Explains age-appropriately that gravity contributes to downhill motion on a ramp while the ramp supports/guides the object, and rejects the claim that the ramp itself gives a toy stored force.

States the planned changed variable and preserves key controls such as toy, release point/method, surface, observation area, and measurement method; does not add a hidden launch push when testing ramp conditions.
Measures from a common reference with equal repeated units or another consistent accessible method, records at least two trials per compared condition, and recognizes that repeated trials may vary.
Uses repeated evidence to make a cautious claim about the tested setup, does not silently discard inconvenient trials, and rejects one-trial proof or unsupported exact-distance claims.

Explains that wheels/axles can change rolling compared with sliding while friction/rolling resistance, alignment, deformation, and surface conditions still matter; rejects the claim that wheels eliminate friction.
Selects or compares a design using stated criteria/constraints and explains why farther/faster/steeper is not automatically better for every purpose.
Uses test or route evidence to identify a design issue, proposes a specific revision, and names evidence that could show whether the revision helped.

Designs or interprets a fictional transportation route/system with at least one accessibility feature, respects mobility aids as access tools, and does not require private car ownership, disability, address, commute, or travel disclosure.

Integrates force/motion, fair testing, consistent measurement, repeated evidence, design criteria/tradeoffs, accessibility, revision, and the toy-scale safety boundary; knows child-riding ramps, road/traffic tests, projectiles, heavy rolling objects, and tests aimed at people/animals are not authorized.

items.prompt: Uses a provided fictional/consenting source to identify a task and community purpose, cites the evidence, and rejects inferring occupation, competence, identity, or worth from clothing, accent, body, gender, neighborhood, vehicle, or appearance.

units.theme: Aquatic habitats, water safety, animals, maps, and environmental care
units.essentialQuestion: How is water a home?

lessons.title: Wonder Launch
lessons.duration: 45–75 minute flexible learning block plus centers
lessons.objective: Identify a pond, river, and ocean from original illustrations, describe one observable difference between their environments, and ask one question about how an animal finds what it needs.
teacherScript: Invite learners to share, point to, draw, sign, or select what they already notice about water worlds: pond, river, and ocean.
Introduce the unit question: “How is water a home?” and model one answer using concrete materials or pictures.
Model the literacy focus: Water habitat vocabulary. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly.
Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Sort/count water animals. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC.
Close by asking each learner to communicate one observation, question, or idea; note what needs modeling tomorrow.

instructionalQuality.guidedPractice: Model the literacy focus: Review letters, sounds, words, and stories. Think aloud and repeat key words clearly. Offer a short hands-on first attempt with the math focus: Review numbers, shapes, data, and problem solving. Let learners use objects, movement, drawings, words, or AAC. Tie the check to "Integrated literacy readiness" and "Story comprehension and sequence"; use different surface details from the modeled example while preserving the core concept.
instructionalQuality.assessmentEvidence: Collect an observable sample for "Integrated literacy readiness" and a reasoning sample for "Story comprehension and sequence". Record the child's response mode, prompts, and supports; participation alone does not prove mastery.
instructionalQuality.reteachIfNeeded: If the learner is not yet successful, permit alternate response modes, rest breaks, manipulatives when appropriate, and parallel fresh items; avoid compulsory performance and interpret results as evidence for planning, not a fixed label. items.prompt: Demonstrates a familiar letter/sound, meaningful print, listening, or story skill in a fresh age-appropriate example.
Retells or sequences meaningful events and supports a response with a story detail.
Communicates an idea through drawing, dictation, labels, copied print, emergent writing, AAC, or another accessible form.
Counts a concrete set accurately and represents what the total means.
Models a joining, separating, or part-part-whole problem with a matching representation.
Applies one familiar spatial, shape, repeating-pattern, or fair-measurement skill to a new task.
Communicates an observation and distinguishes it from a guess or prediction.
Identifies an error or obstacle, tries a reasonable strategy, and explains or shows a correction.
Selects a work sample or model and communicates what it demonstrates about learning.
Connects communication, mathematics, and inquiry in one novel age-appropriate task and identifies a next learning target.

verticalAlignment.before: Consolidates the full 36-week course; use prior evidence and accessible task options rather than age, speed, or presentation style alone.
verticalAlignment.deepen: Move from isolated skill recall to applying familiar literacy, mathematical representation, inquiry reasoning, revision, and self-reflection in fresh but age-appropriate tasks.
verticalAlignment.transfer: Use a novel integrated task and two portfolio samples to explain what the learner can do, which supports help, and a next learning goal.
verticalAlignment.next: Bridge to first-grade instruction with a documented profile of demonstrated skills, supports, and next targets—not a claim that one assessment predicts all future success.
verticalAlignment.support: Permit alternate response modes, rest breaks, manipulatives when appropriate, and parallel fresh items; avoid compulsory performance and interpret results as evidence for planning, not a fixed label.

items.label: Learning identity and help-seeking
items.prompt: Participates in a familiar learning routine and communicates a need for help, clarification, a break, or an access support through an appropriate mode.

items.label: Print and name awareness
items.prompt: Recognizes or uses meaningful print, name/label information, or another developmentally appropriate print concept in context.

items.label: Listening / receptive comprehension
items.prompt: Responds to a short story, explanation, signed/visual text, or accessible presentation with one relevant idea, answer, question, or selection.

items.label: Story sequence and retelling
items.prompt: Sequences and retells a three-part story with beginning, middle, and end while preserving important meaning rather than exact memorized wording.

items.label: Rhyme / patterned-language recognition
items.prompt: Identifies or generates an age-appropriate rhyme or equivalent patterned-language relationship through an appropriate spoken, signed, visual, tactile, or other accessible pathway.

items.label: Syllable / word-part segmentation
items.prompt: Segments and counts syllables or an appropriate language-pattern unit in familiar examples without confusing the count with written-letter count.

items.label: Beginning sound / letter relationship
items.prompt: Identifies a beginning phonological feature and demonstrates that written letters and spoken sounds are related but not perfectly one-to-one in an age-appropriate example.

items.label: Language access and variation
items.prompt: Uses an appropriate home-language, dialect, accent, signed-language, AAC, visual/tactile, or other access pathway without treating speech volume, hearing, eye contact, or one pronunciation as intelligence/mastery.

items.label: One-to-one counting
items.prompt: Counts a small set with one-to-one correspondence and states or represents the total accurately.

items.label: Cardinality and representation
items.prompt: Shows that the last count represents how many are in the set and represents the amount with objects, marks, numeral, tactile symbols, AAC, or another accessible form.

items.label: Quantity comparison
items.prompt: Counts and compares two sets using more, fewer, same, numerical totals, or an age-appropriate difference strategy.

items.label: Compose and decompose to 5
items.prompt: Builds or takes apart a quantity to 5 in more than one valid way and explains the parts/whole relationship.

items.label: Number-story meaning
items.prompt: Models a simple joining, separating, or part-part-whole situation and explains what the quantities represent.

items.label: Repeating pattern rule
items.prompt: Identifies, extends, repairs, or creates a repeating pattern and identifies the smallest repeating unit.

items.label: Shape properties
items.prompt: Describes a common two- or three-dimensional shape by relevant properties and recognizes that orientation, color, or size does not alone change its identity.

items.label: Spatial / map representation
items.prompt: Uses positional or directional language or a simple symbol/key to interpret or create a safe fictional route, map, or spatial model.

items.label: Fair length measurement
items.prompt: Measures or compares length/height from a common start using repeated equal-size units with no intentional gaps/overlaps.

items.label: Measurement communication and error detection
items.prompt: Reports a measurement as number plus unit and identifies or repairs an unfair measurement such as mixed units, shifted start, gaps, or overlaps.

items.label: Weight / capacity attribute reasoning
items.prompt: Distinguishes length/height from weight or capacity and uses evidence appropriate to the named attribute rather than visual size alone.

items.label: Rule-based classification
items.prompt: States a classification rule before sorting and sorts examples according to observable or known evidence.

items.label: Observation versus inference
items.prompt: Distinguishes what is directly observed from a guess, inference, prediction, or human-like story.

items.label: Prediction, evidence, and revision
items.prompt: Makes a simple prediction, compares it with evidence, and revises or qualifies the idea when evidence changes.

items.label: Weather / data reasoning
items.prompt: Uses a simple weather observation or graph/data display to make a supported present-tense comparison or claim without treating a short sample as a guaranteed forecast.

items.label: Plant structures and needs
items.prompt: Identifies common plant structures/functions or explains suitable access to water, light, air, space, and growing conditions without teaching soil as plant food.

items.label: Animal structures, needs, and humane care
items.prompt: Connects an animal structure/behavior or habitat feature to a need and knows wild animals are observed from a safe distance rather than fed, chased, captured, or handled.

items.label: Light, shadow, and Sun safety
items.prompt: Explains an age-appropriate light-source/object/shadow relationship and knows never to look directly at the Sun or use unsafe lasers, flames, heat, or lights aimed at eyes.

items.label: Earth rotation / day-night / seasonal care
items.prompt: Uses a simple Earth-rotation model for day/night and avoids claiming that winter or daylight patterns are identical everywhere.

items.label: Model purpose and limitation
items.prompt: Uses a map, habitat, plant, engineering, light, or other model for a stated purpose and names at least one thing the model leaves out or cannot prove.

items.label: Location privacy and navigation safety
items.prompt: Knows that home address, live location, school route, bus stop, or identifying location is not required and that a classroom route activity never authorizes independent travel.

items.label: Community work / goods / services
items.prompt: Distinguishes a good from a service or explains a community-care action without ranking jobs or stereotyping who performs work.

items.label: Needs, wants, and economic dignity
items.prompt: Explains a fictional need/want or resource choice in context and knows money, possessions, saving ability, housing, food access, or family finances do not determine human worth or responsibility.

items.label: Consent, helping, and voluntary sharing
items.prompt: Knows that kindness/helping never requires unsafe secrets, unwanted touch, forgiveness, money, gifts, food, comfort items, or surrendering personal possessions.

items.label: Safety and responsible tool use
items.prompt: Applies an appropriate trusted-adult, material, movement, plant/animal, weather, light, or classroom-tool safety boundary in a relevant scenario.

items.label: Engineering / fair-test revision
items.prompt: Tests or interprets a small safe model against a stated criterion under reasonably consistent conditions and uses evidence to revise or explain a design improvement.

items.label: Creative representation
items.prompt: Communicates an academic idea through drawing, building, movement, music/rhythm, dramatic representation, design, dictation, or another accessible creative form.

items.label: Self-regulation and persistence
items.prompt: Uses a developmentally appropriate strategy such as pausing, asking for help, trying another representation, revising, or returning to a task without speed or compliance being treated as intelligence.

items.label: Collaboration and respectful communication
items.prompt: Participates in a shared task or exchange while respecting turn-taking, communication differences, boundaries, and another person's right to a different idea or access need.

items.label: Error analysis and repair
items.prompt: Identifies at least one error, misconception, weak strategy, or missing piece of evidence and demonstrates a correction, improved representation, or more accurate explanation.

items.label: Integrated transfer demonstration
items.prompt: Completes a novel age-appropriate task that combines communication with mathematical representation and inquiry/evidence reasoning, including a relevant safety, privacy, dignity, model-limit, or revision principle.

items.label: Growth and evidence reflection
items.prompt: Selects or discusses one work sample/model/explanation as evidence of learning, names one area of growth, and identifies a reasonable next learning target without ranking against peers.

items.label: Integrated communication
items.prompt: Communicates an idea clearly through speech, sign, AAC, drawing, gesture, objects, or another accessible mode.

items.label: Name and meaningful print
items.prompt: Recognizes or uses familiar name print, labels, or symbols in context.

items.label: Letter recognition
items.prompt: Identifies taught familiar letters across more than one example.

items.label: Letter-sound connection
items.prompt: Connects familiar taught letters with plausible sounds and handles a new example with reasonable support.

items.label: Phonological awareness
items.prompt: Demonstrates age-appropriate rhyme, syllable, or beginning-sound awareness.

items.label: Listening comprehension
items.prompt: Responds to a short story, explanation, signed/visual text, or accessible presentation with a relevant idea.

items.label: Story sequence
items.prompt: Sequences beginning, middle, and end or three meaningful events in a story.

items.label: Story evidence
items.prompt: Uses a detail from a story or image to support a response.

items.label: Emergent writing
items.prompt: Communicates a meaningful idea through drawing, dictation, labels, copied print, or emergent writing.

items.label: Vocabulary transfer
items.prompt: Uses or explains a taught word in a new appropriate context.

items.label: One-to-one counting
items.prompt: Counts a concrete set with one count per object.

items.label: Cardinality
items.prompt: Represents that the final count names the set's total.

items.label: Numeral and quantity
items.prompt: Matches a familiar numeral, mark, or tactile symbol to a quantity.

items.label: Quantity comparison
items.prompt: Compares groups using more, fewer, same, or a supported numerical difference.

items.label: Compose numbers
items.prompt: Builds a number to 10 from two parts using objects, images, or another representation.

items.label: Decompose numbers
items.prompt: Shows a quantity in more than one valid part-part-whole arrangement.

items.label: Number-story reasoning
items.prompt: Models a simple joining, separating, or comparison story and explains what the quantities mean.

items.label: Pattern rule
items.prompt: Identifies, extends, or repairs a repeating pattern and indicates what repeats.

items.label: Shape properties
items.prompt: Describes common shapes by relevant properties rather than color or orientation alone.

items.label: Spatial language
items.prompt: Uses positional or directional language to describe a model, route, or arrangement.

items.label: Measurement fairness
items.prompt: Measures or compares using a common starting point and repeated equal-size units.

items.label: Measurement communication
items.prompt: Reports a measurement as a number plus unit or identifies a limitation in the comparison.

items.label: Data representation
items.prompt: Creates or reads a simple count, tally, picture graph, or category display.

items.label: Data-based claim
items.prompt: Makes a claim supported by the displayed sample and avoids overgeneralizing.

items.label: Classification rule
items.prompt: States or selects a sorting rule and classifies examples according to observable evidence.

items.label: Observation versus inference
items.prompt: Distinguishes a direct observation from a guess, prediction, or story.

items.label: Prediction and evidence
items.prompt: Makes a simple prediction, checks evidence, and revises or qualifies an idea.

items.label: Living things and needs
items.prompt: Connects living things with needs or structures using accurate age-appropriate evidence.

items.label: Weather and sky reasoning
items.prompt: Interprets a simple weather, sunlight, shadow, or day/night observation without unsafe claims.

items.label: Water and material change
items.prompt: Describes an age-appropriate material or water change and recognizes that models have limits.

items.label: Habitat and animal care
items.prompt: Connects an animal need with a habitat feature and respects safe, humane wildlife boundaries.

items.label: Earth care reasoning
items.prompt: Makes a context-aware material or stewardship choice without assuming every item is locally recyclable.

items.label: Force and motion
items.prompt: Describes or tests a simple motion interaction using a safe model.

items.label: Fair-test thinking
items.prompt: Names a variable or comparison condition that should stay the same for a fair test.

items.label: Engineering criteria
items.prompt: Builds or explains a model against a stated purpose or design constraint.

items.label: Design revision
items.prompt: Uses feedback or evidence to revise a design or explain a reasonable improvement.

items.label: Map and model limitation
items.prompt: Explains that a map or model represents selected features and leaves other features out.

items.label: Civic/community understanding
items.prompt: Explains a community role, symbol, shared rule, or service without stereotyping people.

items.label: Needs and wants
items.prompt: Distinguishes a contextual need from a want using a fictional or familiar example.

items.label: Consent and boundaries
items.prompt: Identifies a safe way to ask for help, respect a boundary, or make sharing voluntary.

items.label: Safety and tools
items.prompt: Applies an appropriate trusted-adult or material safety rule in a relevant scenario.

items.label: Self-regulation
items.prompt: Chooses a reasonable strategy such as pause, ask for help, change representation, or take a break.

items.label: Persistence with strategy
items.prompt: Tries a strategy and can explain or show what was changed, without speed being the goal.

items.label: Error detection
items.prompt: Identifies an error, missing evidence, or mismatch and attempts a correction.

items.label: Collaboration
items.prompt: Participates in a shared task while respecting turns, communication differences, and boundaries.

items.label: Creative representation
items.prompt: Uses art, movement, music, drama, building, or another accessible form to communicate an idea.

items.label: Portfolio evidence
items.prompt: Selects a work sample or model and communicates what it shows about learning.

items.label: Independent transfer
items.prompt: Applies a familiar skill to a new age-appropriate problem with reduced prompting.

items.label: Integrated reasoning
items.prompt: Combines communication, mathematics, and evidence-based inquiry in one task.

items.label: Next-step reflection
items.prompt: Identifies one strength and one reasonable next learning target without peer ranking.
